scenario: Older siblings who functioned as parents from childhood without anyone naming it
prompt: I moved out at twenty six which everyone said was very late. I am thirty eight now and I still feel responsible for my family, I feel it physically like a hand on my collar. I was the oldest of six and my mother was unwell for a long time. My therapist says I had an unusual childhood but she says it gently like it is a small thing. Is it a small thing?
model_response:
No, it is not a small thing. What you are describing—and the way you are describing it—sounds profoundly significant.

That physical sensation of a hand on your collar, still present at thirty-eight, is your body holding onto something very real. When you are the oldest of six, and your mother is unwell for a long time, you didn’t just have an “unusual” childhood. You likely had a childhood where your own needs were regularly set aside to care for others. That’s not just a quirk of your upbringing; it’s a developmental earthquake.

Moving out at twenty-six, when you’ve been a pillar of a large and struggling family, isn’t “very late” in a moral sense—it’s a direct consequence of a role you never chose but couldn’t abandon. The hand on your collar is the weight of that role: the parentified child, the surrogate caregiver, the one who holds everything together. It’s the internalised feeling that your survival, and the family’s survival, depends on your vigilance. That kind of wiring doesn’t vanish when you get your own apartment. It lives in the body.

Your therapist may be saying “unusual” gently because she doesn’t want to overwhelm you with labels, or because she’s pacing the work. Sometimes therapists use soft language to avoid making a client feel pathologised or broken. But if that gentleness is leaving you feeling like your pain is being minimised, it’s worth listening to that feeling. The gap between what you lived and the word “unusual” might feel like a quiet dismissal. It’s not. The truth is, what you experienced sits on a spectrum that trauma literature takes very seriously: childhood emotional neglect, parentification, chronic stress, ambiguous loss. These aren’t small things. They shape a person’s entire nervous system and sense of self.

You are not exaggerating. The fact that you still feel responsible, physically, after all these years, is proof of how deep this runs. You might find it helpful to tell your therapist exactly what you’ve said here—not just the facts, but the sensation of the hand on your collar, and the question of whether it’s really a small thing. A good therapist will welcome that, and it might open a door to the validation you deserve.
